title: Reliable instruction-following physical work in unfamiliar everyday environments

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a robot system that takes an ordinary-language goal and reliably finishes an unfamiliar, multi-step physical job in an everyday environment the developers did not instrument. It would work without per-task fine-tuning, human coaching, or resets between steps. The capability includes interpreting the goal, choosing and sequencing actions, tracking how its actions change the scene, recognizing mistakes, and recovering until the specified job is finished.

One unchanged policy system could contain a fixed hierarchy of planners, reasoning models, perception systems, and motor controllers. The requirement concerns the competence of the complete system; it does not require a single monolithic neural controller. Its defining advance would be dependable completion of unfamiliar jobs within its physical capabilities, rather than success at isolated movements or separately prompted steps.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would make physical skills reusable through instructions, reducing the programming, task-specific training, and supervision needed to put a robot to work. The supplied research already reports instruction-mediated manipulation and transfer between settings or embodiments. Extending those components to reliable whole-job completion would change the practical unit of interaction from directing individual actions to specifying an outcome. The analogy with reusable computation is a reasoned assessment of the proposed breakthrough, not a demonstrated equivalence.

As a conditional consequence, robots could perform unfamiliar jobs within their demonstrated manipulation and environment scope. Tidying, machine tending, packing, and light assembly are potential applications, especially where existing grippers or simple hands already provide adequate physical capability. A successful home evaluation would support claims about the tested home activities; extending the result to workplaces, different materials, or more demanding equipment would require additional validation. A finite set of successful jobs would establish demonstrated breadth, not universal physical competence.

Practical deployment would still depend on cost, battery endurance, maintenance, and safe interaction with people. Reliable task completion would not itself establish human-level hand dexterity or safety certification. The supplied review identifies a separate Gemini Robotics 2 safety report dated 29 July 2026 whose evaluation excludes the underlying functional safety architecture, reinforcing the distinction between demonstrated competence and a complete case for safe physical deployment.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target is dependable composition of physical skills into unfamiliar jobs without task-specific adaptation or coaching. The supplied sources report substantial components of this capability, but do not establish its full proposed scope. In particular, the π0.7 account distinguishes following unfamiliar instructions from autonomously completing some unfamiliar longer tasks: for those tasks, step-by-step coaching supplies data used to train a high-level language policy. Gemini Robotics 2 reports multi-step execution and self-correction, but the supplied account does not establish the proposed independent, shift-length evaluation.

As an engineering synthesis, a central difficulty is compositional generalization under physical interaction. A system must connect language to the actual objects and their states, order actions around dependencies, and update its plan when contact, clutter, or its own movements alter the scene. Opening an articulated appliance, manipulating a deformable object, and recovering from an unsuccessful grasp require different forms of state estimation and control. These are interacting barriers, not an experimentally established explanation of a single bottleneck.

Another engineering requirement is maintaining reliability across an entire job. Correctly following several individual instructions does not establish that all necessary steps will succeed together, that the intended outcome will be recognized, or that failures will be repaired without help. Evaluation must therefore distinguish component accuracy from whole-job success and autonomous recovery. It must also characterize task novelty: the π0.7 authors acknowledge difficulty quantifying how novel their test instructions are, which limits conclusions about generalization.

current_state.text: Physical Intelligence and colleagues report π0.7 in the arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.15483v2, revised 24 April 2026. According to the supplied review, it follows instructions in unseen kitchens and bedrooms and transfers laundry folding to a target robot without laundry-folding data from that embodiment. That result concerns transfer across embodiments; it does not mean the overall system had no laundry-training experience. The paper also reports performance competitive with specialist policies on espresso-making, laundry, and box-building without task-specific post-training of the generalist. Those comparison tasks were represented in training, including specialist rollout data, so these comparisons do not establish performance on wholly unseen jobs.

The supplied review of Figure 9's caption records sequences of 3–6 open-ended instructions across four unseen kitchens and two unseen bedrooms. The reported metric is the percentage of instructions correctly followed, rather than whole-job success over an extended work period. All tested manipulators use parallel-jaw grippers, and the authors state that instruction novelty is difficult to quantify. For some unfamiliar longer tasks, including toasting a bagel, step-by-step coaching is followed by training a high-level language policy for subsequent autonomous execution. These results support instruction following, transfer, and some multi-step execution, while preserving an important distinction between an unchanged system completing a new job and a system gaining that capability through coaching-derived training.

Carolina Parada's Google DeepMind article, dated 30 July 2026, reports that Gemini Robotics 2 uses the same vision-language-action checkpoint across several embodiments, including humanoid whole-body control spanning walking and manipulation. A separate embodied reasoning model supports task sequences lasting several minutes and involving hundreds of decisions, with reported self-correction when a step fails. The article also states that multi-finger dexterous manipulation remains challenging. Its adaptation claim applies specifically to the On-Device 2 model: adaptation to new bi-arm embodiments takes a few hours, typically using fewer than 200 examples. This is a reported adaptation result, not evidence of immediate deployment on a new body without additional data.

Together, these developer-reported results demonstrate relevant progress in manipulation, cross-embodiment transfer, grounded instruction following, and multi-step execution. Describing all of the achieved capability as short-horizon would understate the reported longer-task results. Nevertheless, the supplied review does not establish an independently scored evaluation of unfamiliar whole jobs over a defined shift, using an unchanged system without coaching or task-specific adaptation. It also does not establish that no other system has met that scope.

The evidence available here has specific limits. The supplied review used π0.7 text that ends within Appendix A-G; its relevant main-text passages and captions were available, but figure graphics and videos were not inspected. The DeepMind article's extracted text was complete, and the linked safety report supplied all 18 pages of text, but its figure graphics were not inspected. Numerical plot results therefore cannot be independently assessed from this record. The supplied freshness-search record is empty, leaving field-wide status as of 1 November 2026 unverified. These limitations constrain interpretation; they do not establish that the reported results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: an independent team evaluates one unchanged policy system in unfamiliar homes that the developers did not instrument. Ordinary-language goals specify finished jobs. The task suite includes clutter, articulated appliances, and at least one deformable object. Jobs last on the order of tens of minutes, and the suite explicitly includes recoverable execution errors so that autonomous recovery is tested rather than inferred from duration. Completion requires achieving the specified outcome without human coaching or resets between steps.
completion_criteria.label: Independent evaluation: unchanged policy completes unfamiliar home jobs without coaching or resets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement and reproducibility requirements: before evaluation, specify task-selection procedures, success thresholds, intervention rules, and the duration of a shift of jobs. Report whole-job success, human interventions, failures, safety incidents, and whether recovery succeeded. Document the fixed system configuration, its training and adaptation exposure, and the basis for calling environments and jobs unfamiliar. Independent repetition across additional homes and task variations would make the result more convincing and help distinguish repeatable competence from favorable task selection.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-specify protocol and report whole-job outcomes, exposure, and unfamiliarity basis

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report which objects, loads, appliance types, environmental conditions, and manipulation demands the demonstration covers. A resident's willingness to leave the robot unsupervised is an intended practical outcome, not a reproducible success threshold or a substitute for safety certification. Home results should support claims about their demonstrated scope; workplace competence requires corresponding workplace evaluations. No finite test suite can establish literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Report covered scope without universality, workplace competence, or safety certification

related_concepts.text: Within the supplied roster, ROB-02, Autonomous dexterous tool use and in-hand manipulation at human reliability, concerns the quality and versatility of manipulation itself. ROB-01 concerns completing unfamiliar jobs, potentially using parallel-jaw grippers or simple hands where those suffice. Better dexterity could broaden its task range, but dependable instruction following does not establish a universal hand. ROB-07, Predictive contact mechanics that plans real manipulation, could supply better predictions for action selection and recovery; it addresses a supporting planning capability rather than the complete language-to-job system.

ROB-09, Lifelong on-robot learning that retains and composes physical skills, overlaps through skill composition and adaptation. ROB-01's proposed evaluation fixes the system and excludes per-task fine-tuning, whereas ROB-09 concerns acquiring and retaining capabilities over time. A robot could learn skills before an ROB-01 evaluation, but success on that evaluation would not by itself establish lifelong retention or learning without interference. Embodied common sense overlaps ROB-01 wherever choosing, sequencing, and repairing actions requires grounded reasoning; it is not a separate entry in the supplied roster.

ROB-03, An artificial muscle that can serve as the main actuator of a useful robot, concerns actuation hardware that could improve a robot's physical implementation. ROB-05, Load-bearing robotic matter that reforms into working machines, concerns reconfigurable material and machine structure. Neither is required by ROB-01's identity, and neither would by itself supply reliable instruction following or unfamiliar-job completion.

ROB-04, Closed-loop robotic self-reproduction from feedstock, and ROB-08, Robot collectives that build functional structures from bulk material, overlap with ROB-01 in autonomous sequencing and physical execution. Their defining outcomes are respectively reproduction and collective construction. Completing everyday jobs would not establish either outcome, and success at a specialized construction or reproduction process would not establish broad competence in unfamiliar homes.

ROB-06, Untethered intervention at a target inside the living human body, and ROB-10, Completion of full surgical procedures on living patients, concern distinct medical settings and outcomes. They can share requirements for perception, planning, manipulation, and recovery, but evidence from everyday environments cannot establish performance inside the body or competence to complete surgery. These entries remain separate from ROB-01.

unresolved_issues: Whether any system had demonstrated the full proposed capability by 1 November 2026 remains unverified because the supplied freshness-search record is empty.
The degree of novelty of π0.7's test instructions remains difficult to quantify; the supplied material does not resolve task-level independence from training exposure.
The π0.7 extraction ends within Appendix A-G, and figure graphics and videos were not inspected in the supplied review. Additional numerical or visual conclusions cannot be resolved from this record.
The proposed evaluation still requires concrete choices for task sampling, shift duration, success thresholds, intervention rules, and reproducibility procedures; these are not established standards.
The task and environment breadth needed to justify unsupervised use, and the separate safety and economic requirements for deployment, remain open.

brief.title: Robots that reliably finish unfamiliar everyday jobs
possible: You could ask a robot to finish tidying a room, rather than direct each movement. In an unfamiliar home without specially installed equipment, it would work out the steps, notice mistakes and recover until the job was done.
The same system could take on new jobs within its physical abilities, without extra training for each task, human coaching or someone resetting it between steps.
why: People could put robots to work by describing an outcome. That would reduce the programming, training and supervision needed to reuse physical skills across different jobs.

Homes and workplaces could use this capability for tidying, tending machines, packing and light assembly. The practical change would be asking for finished work instead of managing individual actions.

sources.showed: The team’s preprint reports instruction following in unfamiliar rooms and laundry folding on a robot body never trained for that task. Some unfamiliar longer jobs required coaching followed by further training.
sources.quote: can enable zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer, making it possible to transfer dexterous tasks such as folding a t-shirt to a robot that was never trained to perform any laundry folding task, matching the performance of expert operators teleoperating the robot on their initial attempts.
sources.cited_for: It supports following instructions in unfamiliar settings and transferring learned skills between robot bodies.
sources.not_established: It does not establish reliable completion of unfamiliar whole jobs by an unchanged system without coaching.

sources.showed: The team reports shared robot control software across different bodies, including walking and handling objects. Its planning system supports tasks lasting several minutes and correction after failed steps.
sources.quote: In this update, we are enabling robots to more reliably execute longer task sequences, lasting several minutes and involving hundreds of decisions.
sources.cited_for: It supports extended task execution, progress tracking and recovery after failed steps.
sources.not_established: It does not establish independent testing of unfamiliar whole jobs across a defined work period without task-specific adaptation.

shown: Physical Intelligence’s π0.7 follows instructions in unfamiliar kitchens and bedrooms and transfers laundry folding between robot bodies. The preprint measures individual instructions; some new longer jobs depend on coaching and further training.

Google DeepMind reports that Gemini Robotics 2 combines walking and object handling across robot bodies. A separate planning system supports multi-step jobs and self-correction. These are developer-reported results.
missing: Independent testing of an unchanged system completing unfamiliar whole jobs without coaching, extra training or resets remains needed.
Whole-job results must establish that robots recognize completion and recover from mistakes throughout an extended work period.
Tests must distinguish genuinely unfamiliar jobs from variations of tasks encountered during training.

milestones.label: An unchanged robot independently finishes unfamiliar home jobs
milestones.explanation: Independent tests in unfamiliar, uninstrumented homes would have to show jobs lasting tens of minutes amid clutter, appliances and flexible objects, with recovery and no coaching or resets. This would establish sustained job completion.

milestones.label: Repeatable tests measure whole jobs and disclose prior training
milestones.explanation: A protocol set beforehand would define success and a work period, then report outcomes, interventions, recovery, safety incidents and prior training. Repetition in other homes would test reliability and unfamiliarity.

milestones.label: Results clearly define the robot’s demonstrated limits
milestones.explanation: Results would have to specify tested objects, loads, appliances, conditions and handling demands. This would bound home claims without implying universal ability, workplace competence or safety certification.

uncertain: How unfamiliar the tested instructions and jobs are relative to training remains difficult to measure.
Task selection, work-period length, success thresholds and intervention rules still need concrete definitions.
The breadth needed for unsupervised use, and the separate safety and economic requirements for deployment, remain open.

page.title: Zero-shot language-conditioned robotic manipulation
page.definition: A fixed robot system completes unfamiliar, multi-step household jobs in previously unseen homes from ordinary-language goals, without intermediate human instructions, physical assistance or resets. Execution is zero-shot: it requires no task-specific training.

goal.need: Housework and food preparation account for recurring physical work. The 2025 US American Time Use Survey interviewed approximately 6,100 people aged 15 or older; its population averages appear below. The robotics goal is to reuse learned physical skills through instructions without collecting action demonstrations for each new job.

figures.caption: Time spent on household activities in the United States, 2025
figures.note: Subcategories are included in the total. Averages include nonparticipants and related travel. BLS adjusted weights for missing shutdown-period diaries.

statements.body: Japan Science and Technology Agency, Moonshot Goal 3
statements.quote: For that purpose, robots must be able to learn and act on their own through the co-evolution of AI and robots.
statements.context: The programme connects this capability to work at understaffed sites and assistance in everyday life.

statements.quote: From feet to fingertips — we are teaching robots intelligent whole-body control, fine dexterity, and teamwork to complete a broad range of complex tasks
performing new tasks has proven elusive.
statements.context: The passage concerns composing skills encountered during training into new tasks.

completion.title: Independent researchers replicate zero-shot completion of unfamiliar household jobs.
completion.criterion: Independent researchers reproduce one unchanged robot system completing unfamiliar, multi-step jobs in previously unseen homes without installed task aids. Jobs require skill combinations not represented as complete jobs in task-specific training. Every goal-specified final state is reached without additional training, intermediate human instructions, physical assistance or resets. At least one completed job includes autonomous recovery from an execution failure. The demonstrated scope is confined to the independently tested jobs and conditions.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional criterion; no combined external pass test located.
completion.basis: RoboCup@Home rules, CALVIN, HomeRobot, JST Moonshot Goal 3, NIST's humanoid benchmark and developer evaluations were searched for a fixed-system, unfamiliar-job completion test. No accessible document located combines these conditions with a numerical reliability threshold. Independently replicated whole-job execution is the proposed minimum demonstration; it does not establish a population-wide success rate.

milestones.title: A simulated robot completes five consecutive CALVIN manipulation instructions.
milestones.criterion: Complete all five subtasks of a feasible CALVIN instruction chain, satisfying each simulator state-based success condition before receiving the next instruction. The published evaluation contains 1,000 chains drawn from 34 tasks; resets occur between chains. The original MCIL baseline reported 0.08% full-chain success with training and testing in environment D, and 0% when trained in A–C and tested in D. This tests instructed subtask composition in simulation.
milestones.set_by: Mees and colleagues, CALVIN long-horizon evaluation, section III-C.2.
milestones.threshold_quote: We treat the 34 tasks of the previous evaluation as subgoals and compute valid sequences consisting of five sequential tasks.

milestones.title: A real robot completes all four HomeRobot fetch-and-place stages within 300 timesteps.
milestones.criterion: Complete FindObj, Pick, FindRec and Place in one real-robot episode of at most 300 timesteps: reach within 1 m of the visible object, grasp it, reach within 1 m of the visible destination receptacle, and place the object stably. Test object instances are absent from training. In a controlled three-room apartment, the original Stretch benchmark reported 4 successful episodes out of 20 for its reinforcement-learning baseline and 3 out of 20 for its heuristic baseline.
milestones.set_by: HomeRobot authors, real-world benchmark and Appendix C.2.
milestones.threshold_quote: The episode is considered to have succeeded if it succeeds in all 4 stages.

milestones.title: A robot opens an air fryer, loads a sweet potato and closes it without live coaching.
milestones.criterion: Achieve all four points in π0.7's Loading an Air Fryer rubric: open the appliance, pick up the sweet potato, put it in the basket and close the appliance. The evaluation allows a high-level language policy trained from task-specific coaching episodes. The preprint reports autonomous policies for five tasks after this training; it does not establish zero-shot execution of those complete jobs. The result is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Physical Intelligence, π0.7 sections IX-D and A-G; task-specific experimental rubric.
milestones.threshold_quote: Open an air fryer, place a sweet potato into the basket, and close the air fryer.

milestones.title: A robot places all 13–15 toys into a basket in an unseen home, within 1 minute per toy.
milestones.criterion: In Figure's Living Room Tidy evaluation, place every one of 13–15 scattered toys into the basket. Exceeding the 1-minute limit for any toy aborts the rollout; a safety intervention also aborts and fails it. A fixed checkpoint per task was evaluated across 30 unseen homes. Figure reported 56% whole-task success pooled across tidying, towel folding and bed making; separate task policies had been trained elsewhere. The trial denominator is not disclosed. The result is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Figure, Helix 2.5 evaluation protocol and Detailed Eval Criteria, published 17 September 2026.
milestones.threshold_quote: Living Room Tidy: All 13-15 toys scattered in the scene are picked and placed in the basket.

milestones.title: One unchanged robot system completes an unfamiliar household job and recovers from an execution failure.
milestones.criterion: A developer demonstrates an entire unfamiliar job in a previously unseen home using one fixed system, without task-specific training, intermediate instructions, physical assistance or resets. Every goal-specified final state is reached, including autonomous recovery from an execution failure. HomeBody reports two demonstrated requests in one unseen kitchen without environment-specific learning, but does not establish training independence of the jobs or an audited non-intervention protocol. Its project-page result is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Atlas provisional demonstration criterion; searches of RoboCup@Home, CALVIN, HomeRobot and developer protocols located no common test with this full scope.

results.finding: π0.7 follows live coaching to load a sweet potato into an air fryer; sample size and success rate are not reported in the supplied text.
results.detail: The supplied text describes training a high-level policy from coaching episodes, but does not report an autonomous air-fryer rollout achieving all four rubric points.

results.finding: Apollo 2 completed one illustrated watering-can transfer; the number of trials and success rate were not reported.
results.detail: The example combines navigation and manipulation, but the source does not establish that the setting was an unseen home, that the job was unfamiliar, or that a failure was recovered from during the example. Its general claim of self-correction does not document a specific recovery.
results.quote: Apollo processes the instruction, walks to the table, and picks up the watering can, takes a few steps to the shelves, and places it precisely in its destination.

results.finding: MMaDA-VLA completed all five CALVIN subtasks in 89.7% of 1,000 rollout episodes.
results.detail: The ABC→D evaluation trained on environments A–C and tested in D. The model was fine-tuned for CALVIN.
results.quote: It further achieves an 89.7% success rate on the fifth task, 11.6 percentage points above DreamVLA’s 78.1%.

results.finding: Xiaomi-Robotics-0 completed all five CALVIN tasks in 88.1% of 1,000 instruction chains.
results.detail: In the ABC→D setting, the model was trained on environments A–C and evaluated in environment D under the standard CALVIN protocol.

results.finding: Figure's Helix 2.5 achieved 56% whole-task success across three tasks evaluated in 30 unseen homes.
results.detail: The result pools tidying, towel folding and bed making; the trial denominator and task-specific success rate are undisclosed. Separate task policies were trained elsewhere. Toy rollouts were aborted after a one-minute timeout per toy; safety interventions also failed a rollout.
results.quote: The Index-pretrained policy succeeded on 56% - over 6x higher (Figure 1). Success required completing the entire task: every item tidied, every towel folded, or the whole bed made. We give no partial credit.

results.finding: HomeBody demonstrated 2 household requests in 1 previously unseen kitchen.
results.detail: The page reports no environment-specific training or additional policy learning, but does not establish that the jobs were absent from training or that execution had no intervention or resets. It describes retries, but does not establish that a demonstrated job included recovery from a failure.
results.quote: In a previously unseen kitchen, our system allows a Unitree G1 guided by GPT Astra to clean up across the room and retrieve a remembered object from an underspecified request, without environment-specific training data or additional policy learning.
